implementation_notes: The modern C++ default: a free or static function switches on a tag or on configuration and returns std::unique_ptr<Product>, so callers name only the product type and ownership is explicit at the type level. std::make_unique needs C++14, so on a C++11 toolchain write std::unique_ptr<Product>(new ConcreteProduct(...)). Prefer this over a virtual Creator whenever the set of concrete products is decided at the call site; keep the classic form only when the factory object itself must be polymorphic and swappable at run time.
pitfalls: Returning a raw Product* makes ownership implicit and is the classic leak source; return std::unique_ptr and never the concrete type.
A polymorphic base that will be deleted through needs a virtual destructor: a useful rule is public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual, whenever delete expressions are involved.
Function-local static registries are initialized on first use and destroyed at exit; a factory called from another static initializer can observe a not-yet-built registry.

variants.name: Classic GoF Creator with a virtual create_product()
variants.idiom_name: abstract Creator with virtual create_product() override
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern as published: an abstract Creator declares the factory method (pure virtual, or virtual with a default product) and its ConcreteCreator subclasses override it, which is what 'let a subclass decide' means literally in C++. Dynamic dispatch through the base class works even when the concrete creator type is unknown at compile time, which is exactly the framework-hook case; the cost is a parallel class hierarchy and a vtable call per creation.
pitfalls: Do not call create_product() from Creator's constructor or destructor: during construction the dynamic type is still the base class, so the call resolves to the base version (or stays pure virtual and terminates).
Return-type covariance does not help with smart pointers: std::unique_ptr<Derived> is not covariant with std::unique_ptr<Base>, so every override must return the same smart pointer type.

variants.name: Creator registry of std::function values
variants.implementation_notes: Creation becomes data rather than a class hierarchy: a map from product name to std::function<std::unique_ptr<Product>()> is filled at startup (or by self-registering translation units), and the factory is a lookup. This scales to plugin architectures and keeps each product's creation code next to that product, at the price of type erasure and a runtime miss when a name is not registered; choose it when the set of products is open and comes from separate modules.
pitfalls: std::function has a type-erasure cost (possible allocation for large captures) and an empty state that throws std::bad_function_call - check before invoking if a miss is expected.
Static initialization order across translation units is unspecified; register in one explicit init step rather than in global constructors unless you know the order.
Registrations are process-wide mutable state: they leak between tests and races if a plugin loads on another thread.
